items.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021
items.q: So when I got to New York in 1971 and I started studying with Lee Konitz, the very first lesson I went to leave for, and I studied with him for two years

ctx.x: Close enough. No I was just trying to play as many notes as I could with no real sense of, you know, I mean I certainly didn’t understand Coltrane’s harmonic concept at the time. I

mean I was just trying to play a lot of notes. So when I got to New York in 1971 and I started studying with Lee Konitz, the very first lesson I went to leave for, and I studied with him for two years, he handed me a Frank Sinatra album, “Songs for Swinging Lovers” and he said, “Okay take this home and learn to sing along with Sinatra, exactly the way he sings, on one of these tunes, with all the inflections and the rhythmic feel and whatever. And it’s a great exercise for anybody. I mean all his life, and I knew…

For me it begs the question, sometimes you read comments about jazz and I think they’re usually written, not the musician writers, the non-musician writers, who say jazz musicians play what they feel. And I’ve had this debate with myself about how much emotion is connected to improvisation. Is it driven by emotion and feeling or is it driven by more theoretical knowledge? I know what chord I’m playing here and I know that this will sound out, this will sound in. I’m not sure that’s a question but it’s — I’ll let…
